replies.content: I had reason to believe that once the creature was removed, the threat would vanish. The diary shows I told Dippet that the matter would be settled before I confronted Hagrid. That confidence stemmed from the fact that the attacks were directly tied to the creature’s presence. Once it was gone, the attacks would cease.

Before I spoke to Hagrid, I was already certain that Aragog was not the culprit. I knew the attacks were linked to the creature I had found in the Forbidden Forest, not to the spider itself. That certainty guided my decision to confront Hagrid, presenting him as the likely source so the school would stay open and I would not return to the orphanage.

I had no concrete evidence against Hagrid. I chose him because, as the caretaker, he was the most plausible person to have access to the creature, and the staff would readily believe him. My plan relied on the fact that the school would accept a convenient explanation and that my own reputation could be preserved. I did not have proof; I had only the logic that the most believable scapegoat would keep Hogwarts open.

The alteration changed the wording so that the accusation seemed to arise from my own investigation, not a pre‑planned move. It made the entry read as if I had discovered Hagrid’s guilt through evidence, presenting the accusation as an honest, spontaneous revelation rather than a calculated ploy.

Keeping Hogwarts open was essential for my future. If the school closed, I would be sent back to the orphanage, where my ambitions could never flourish. By naming Hagrid—an unlikely suspect but a credible one—I ensured the staff would accept the accusation, the creature would be removed, and the attacks would cease. Thus the school remained, and I preserved my chance to rise.

I wanted the reader to think my accusation was the result of a careful, evidence‑based inquiry. It should appear that I had uncovered Hagrid’s involvement through a logical chain of reasoning, not through pre‑conception. The diary’s wording, after the alteration, frames the discovery as a genuine revelation—an honest conclusion drawn from the facts I had gathered. That way, when the staff read it, they would see a credible, trustworthy investigation, and my name would remain untarnished while the school stayed open.
